papers.title: Twenty Years at the Crossroads: Is Clinical Cardiac Electrophysiology Science, Procedure, or Both?
"A Literal Form of Torture" - Health Care Stakeholder Perspectives on Sleep and Wellbeing Among First-Time Parents in Ireland During the Postpartum Period.
papers.abstract: Postpartum sleep loss and fatigue are common during the transition to parenthood, with important implications for parental health and wellbeing. Given their role in supporting families during this transition, health care stakeholders can provide valuable insight into the sleep-related challenges experienced by first-time parents. This study employed a narrative inquiry approach to examine health care stakeholders' (e.g. midwives, psychologists, and doulas) perceptions, attitudes, and opinions regarding sleep and wellbeing among first-time parents during the postpartum period. Five semi-structured focus groups (N = 16) were conducted online with stakeholders. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three primary themes were identified: 1) Transition to parenthood, 2) Barriers to parental sleep, and 3) Sleep and biopsychosocial functioning. Theme 1 captured how the unpredictability of sleep postnatally challenged parents' preconcieved expectations, revealing a discrepancy between anticipated and actual postpartum experiences. Theme 2 was concerned with the barriers that prevent first-time parents from securing sleep. Theme 3 described how sleep loss impacts parents' physical, mental, and social wellbeing. Participants agreed that many first-time parents are largely underprepared for the impact that sleep loss can have on their wellbeing. This research has provided evidence for the need for specific perinatal interventions designed to support first-time parents who struggle with the effects of sleep loss. The findings reported here highlight that postpartum sleep loss should be recognised as a significant clinical issue rather than an expected/unavoidable aspect of early parenting. Health care professionals should routinely assess parental sleep quality during perinatal care.

papers.title: Elucidating the relationship between protein amide I, II, and III bands and secondary structures by localized anharmonic vibrational calculations.
papers.abstract: The amide I, II, and III spectra of the insulin dimer and ubiquitin were investigated using our recently developed localized, second-order vibrational quasi-degenerate perturbation theory (VQDPT2) combined with quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics calculations. By averaging over ten snapshots from molecular dynamics trajectories, we confirmed that the computed spectra converged to a sufficient degree. Although the method has intrinsic limitations due to the neglect of vibrational coupling between neighboring amide groups, we found that the method provides a useful basis for spectral analysis of these proteins. The analysis of the averaged amide I, II, and III bands revealed that, for both proteins, the amide II and III peak positions tend to be closely associated with the coil contribution, whereas the origin of the amide I maximum is more protein dependent. The calculated amide I and III frequencies of the coil structures showed good agreement with experimental values. The spectra of each secondary structure were further subdivided according to the type of hydrogen bonding within the secondary structure. For structurally constrained α-helix and β-sheet structures, hydrogen-bond-dependent amide I frequency shifts were found to correlate with changes in the amide dihedral angles (O=C-N-H). Localized VQDPT2 enables direct interpretation of amide band shifts associated with conformational changes and provides a deeper understanding of the structural origin responsible for these band shifts.

papers.title: 6.42 Million Tests Reviewed: Analysis of Critical Value Evolution Characteristics and Therapeutic Drug Monitoring Warning Value in a Psychiatric Hospital Over 10 Years.
papers.abstract: Critical values in laboratory testing and alert values for therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) are essential for clinical safety and psychotropic drug optimization, yet their distribution, associated factors, and clinical significance in psychiatric specialty hospitals remain insufficiently characterized. Therefore, we aimed to determine these parameters to provide a theoretical basis for optimizing critical value management and psychotropic drug use. A retrospective analysis was conducted on critical value reports from the clinical laboratory and TDM alert value data of inpatients and outpatients at the Affiliated Mental Health Center of Kunming Medical University from January 2016 to December 2025. The incidence of critical and TDM alert values, sex and age differences, project composition ratios, and distributions by ward and disease diagnoses were analyzed. A total of 3700 reports of critical and TDM alert values were included with 27.27% older than 65 years (63.49% female and 36.51% male). Among the categories of hematological routine, biochemical, coagulation critical values, and hematological drug concentration monitoring warning values, hematological drug concentration monitoring warning values accounted for the highest proportion. (49.73%) and among individual test items, the top‑five items were: white blood cell count (15.89%), serum potassium (8.87%), myoglobin (7.06%), glucose (6.27%), and TDM venlafaxine and its metabolites (5.81%). The critical and TDM alert values came from the geriatric psychiatry (1220 cases; 32.97%), outpatient (803 cases; 21.70%), and sleep medicine (8.08%) departments. In this psychiatric specialty hospital, Among the categories of hematological routine, biochemical, coagulation critical values, and hematological drug concentration monitoring warning values, hematological drug concentration monitoring warning values accounted for the highest proportion. The predominant individual issues included leukopenia, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and elevated venlafaxine metabolite levels, which may be associated with the adverse effects of psychotropic medications, patient adherence, and comorbid physical illnesses. Individualized critical and TDM alert value thresholds should be determined based on specific characteristics to provide healthcare professionals with reference criteria for assessing disease severity to improve the quality of critical value management and medication use and reducing the incidence of adverse outcomes.

papers.title: Mapping the Research Landscape and Global Trends: A Bibliometric Analysis of Event-related Potential in Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.abstract: There is an urgent need for objective biomarkers to facilitate early diagnosis and dynamic monitoring of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Event-Related Potential (ERP), as a neuroelectrophysiological technique with high temporal resolution, shows great promise in addressing this demand. However, the macro-level developmental trajectory, research status, and frontier directions within this field remain to be systematically elucidated. This study employs bibliometric methods to delineate the development trends, knowledge structures, and research frontiers of ERP applications in AD, thereby offering a novel perspective for early diagnosis, dynamic monitoring, and efficacy assessment. Publications related to ERP and AD were retrieved and screened from the Web of Science Core Collection. A comprehensive quantitative and visual analysis was conducted using Microsoft Excel, CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and the bibliometrix package in R. The analysis covered publication trends, national/institutional collaboration networks, author co-occurrence, core journals, reference and keyword co-occurrence, and clustering. The number of annual publications in this field continued to grow. The United States, China, and Italy were the most productive countries, whereas the cooperation network among institutions and authors was decentralized. Keyword clustering identified six major research topics: P300/N200, Mismatch Negativity (MMN), N170, N400, Olfactory Event-Related Potential (OERP), and Electroencephalography (EEG). An analysis of the global research landscape reveals that ERP research has developed from an exploratory tool in the field of AD to an active research field of neuroscience. Journal and citation analysis indicate that the field has distinct clinical problem-driven features; keyword cluster analysis revealed six major themes corresponding to classical cognitive assessment, early sensory memory, and social cognition. Thematic analysis revealed that MMN and other ERP components that are sensitive to early abnormalities may become future research hotspots; however, the overall cooperation in this field still shows a certain degree of geographical concentration and institutional dispersion. In the future, it is necessary to build a closer international and interdisciplinary cooperation network, establish a standardized ERP evaluation scheme, and embed it throughout the entire process of early identification, staging, and monitoring of the effect of intervention in AD. This research systematically presents the current state of research, hotspots, and evolutionary trends in ERP in the field of AD. The results suggest that in the future, a closer international and interdisciplinary cooperation network and further prospective clinical validation are needed to clarify the diagnostic performance and practical application value of ERP, thereby promoting its clinical application.

papers.title: Greater proximity to greenspace is associated with fewer depressive symptoms among urban middle-aged adults.
papers.abstract: Understanding the factors that influence depression is crucial for both its treatment and prevention. Residential greenspace has received increasing attention for its potential role in mitigating depressive symptoms. However, traditional statistical methods are fundamentally constrained to evaluating simple bivariate associations between greenspace exposure and depression risk, overlooking the complex interactions among key health-related factors and failing to comprehensively assess the relative importance of greenspace compared to other contributing factors. We employed machine learning (ML) methods to assess the effects of multiple factors, including greenspace, on the development of depressive symptoms among 1,542 urban middle-aged adults in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, with depressive symptoms measured using the 10-item Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale. Individual greenspace exposure for each subject was quantified using vegetation indices obtained from the NASA satellite database. Among the five ML models, the Support Vector Machines model achieved the best predictive performance, with an AUC of 0.776. Life satisfaction, EVI250m (a measure of greenspace), social activity, pain, sleep duration, and impairment in instrumental activities of daily living were significant predictors of depressive symptoms. EVI250m, identified by the ML model, indicated that closer proximity to greenspace was associated with a greater reduction in depressive symptoms. Furthermore, Shapley Additive Explanations values confirmed that greenspace ranked among the top influential factors. Residential greenspace is associated with fewer depressive symptoms and ranks prominently among the most influential factors within the examined health-related variables. The potential beneficial association with greenspace appears to be stronger with closer proximity to residential areas.

papers.title: Correction: Cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (CIRBP) adjusts clock-gene expression and REM-sleep recovery following sleep deprivation.
Audience Gaze and Felt Social Connection With Individual Performers During Live Dance.
papers.abstract: In everyday social interactions, our looking behavior reflects our relationships with others, but the role that social perception plays for engagement with the performing arts is understudied. We commissioned the durational, community-focused, 16-h dance performance How Shall We Begin Again?, comprising a continuous relay of individual improvised performances by 50 people over 2 consecutive days. During the performance, we recorded eye movements and mobile EEG from 88 audience members who entered and exited the performance space freely. Audience members reported on their experience of individual performers immediately after leaving the performance space. Gaze toward people in the scene showed a significant indirect association with felt social connection through self-reported focus on individual performers; the overall gaze-connection association, however, was not statistically significant. Individual differences in mind wandering, dance experience, and empathy were associated with gaze and engagement measures, but not with felt social connection. Finally, EEG alpha power decreased and EEG delta/gamma power increased when dance was accompanied by music. Together, these data suggest that engagement with dance depends not only on what is being performed (dance/choreography/music) but also on who is performing, highlighting that dance is an inherently embodied art form that can foster social connections between people.
papers.journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Comparative analysis of pain experience and quality of life in patients with oral lichen planus and burning mouth syndrome.
papers.abstract: Oral lichen planus (OLP) and burning mouth syndrome (BMS) are chronic oral conditions associated with persistent pain, but direct comparisons of their pain profiles and contributing factors remain limited. This study compared factors influencing pain perception between OLP and BMS. This cross-sectional study included 46 patients with OLP and 50 with BMS. Pain characteristics, pain catastrophizing, and quality of life were assessed using the Brief Pain Inventory-Korean version, Pain Catastrophizing Scale-Korean version, and a Korean-language Oral Potentially Malignant Disorders Quality of Life questionnaire. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test; Mann-Whitney U or independent t-tests were applied accordingly, and effect sizes were calculated using Cohen's d. Pain intensity predictors were identified using stepwise multiple linear regression. Patients with BMS reported higher pain intensity (p ≤ 0.003, d = -1.22 to -0.63) and catastrophizing (p = 0.005, d = -0.56) than those with OLP, whereas patients with OLP showed greater mastication-related pain interference (p = 0.002, d = 0.74) and poorer quality of life (p = 0.020, d = 0.50). Regression identified mastication and rumination in OLP (adjusted R2 = 0.419) and sleep disturbance, rumination, and magnification in BMS (adjusted R2 = 0.454) as primary predictors. Age stratification revealed an opposite age-pain relationship: older patients with BMS (>60 years) had higher pain intensity (p < 0.001), whereas younger patients with OLP (≤60 years) reported higher pain intensity (p = 0.037). Pain interference was more interconnected across life domains in OLP (27 correlations with |r| > 0.5) than in BMS (6 correlations). OLP and BMS exhibit distinct pain profiles, with OLP characterized by widespread functional interference influenced by mastication-related and cognitive factors, and BMS marked by higher pain intensity with prominent psychological contributors. Condition-specific strategies incorporating cognitive behavioral therapy targeting rumination may improve pain-related outcomes.
papers.journal: Journal of oral & facial pain and headache

papers.title: Effects of an Esketamine-Containing Induction Regimen on Postoperative Sleep, Analgesia, and Postpartum Depression in Parturients with Sleep Disorders Undergoing Cesarean Section Under General Anesthesia: A Double-Blind Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: Preoperative sleep disturbances in parturients undergoing cesarean section correlate with exacerbated postoperative pain and an elevated risk of postpartum depression. Although esketamine demonstrates analgesic and antidepressant benefits in the general cesarean population, its combined effects on sleep, analgesia, and mood remain poorly characterized in patients with pre-existing sleep impairment. This study investigated the efficacy of an esketamine‑containing induction regimen on postoperative sleep quality, analgesia, and early depressive symptoms in parturients with PSQI‑defined preoperative sleep disorders scheduled for elective cesarean section under general anesthesia. We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 90 parturients scheduled for elective cesarean section under general anesthesia. Participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive either an esketamine-containing induction regimen (esketamine 0.25 mg/kg plus propofol 1.0 mg/kg; n=45) or a standard induction regimen (saline plus propofol 2.0 mg/kg; n=45). All 90 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (missing data imputed), and 84 (41 vs 43) were included in the complete-case sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1, assessed using an 11-point sleep Numerical Rating Scale (NRS; 0=best, 10=worst; 24-hour recall). Secondary outcomes included sleep NRS scores on POD 3 and POD 42, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) on POD 42 (exploratory); Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores at 2, 12, 24, and 48 hours, and rescue analgesic consumption over 72 hours; and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scores on POD 3 and POD 42 (≥13 indicating a positive result). The esketamine regimen significantly improved the primary outcome (sleep NRS on POD 1; mean difference [MD] = 3.0, 95% CI: 2.0 to 4.0; P < 0.001). Exploratory secondary outcomes showed early pain benefits and reduced rescue analgesia (risk ratio [RR] = 3.33, 95% CI: 0.98 to 11.32; absolute risk difference = 15.5%, 95% CI: 0.7% to 30.21%), but these differences were small with wide intervals. Continuous EPDS scores were lower on POD 3 (P = 0.004), while the exploratory binary analysis (EPDS ≥ 13) was not significant (RR = 1.22, 95% CI: 0.56 to 2.66; P = 0.613). No serious adverse events occurred; however, the trial was not powered for safety outcomes. An esketamine-containing induction regimen was associated with improved early sleep quality on POD 1 in parturients with preoperative sleep disorders undergoing cesarean delivery under general anesthesia. However, because the trial was not powered for secondary outcomes or safety, and the differing propofol doses prevent isolation of esketamine's specific effect, these secondary findings are exploratory. Further adequately powered trials are required to confirm these results and evaluate safety. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300078490.

papers.title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation and Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation in Athletes: Optimizing Athletic Performance and Sleep Quality Through Neuromodulation.
papers.abstract: Neuromodulation is a procedure relying on the delivery of specific stimuli to selected sites of the nervous system and hereby influencing its activity. Even though the underlying neurobiological mechanisms are not yet fully elucidated and the research is still ongoing, neuromodulation is already being used as an intervention for various mental conditions and insomnia, or it may even improve the physical performance of athletes. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the effects of specific neuromodulation techniques on performance and sleep quality in athletes, focusing on cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). PubMed, SCOPUS, Web of Science and Ovid MEDLINE databases were searched for relevant articles. All types of publications were taken into account, but original studies, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and meta-analyses were given priority. Current evidence shows that while tDCS may improve athletic performance, especially endurance and sport-specific skills, its impact on sleep in athletes is inconclusive. This method may increase subjectively reported total sleep time and subjective sleep quality, but no objective improvement has been demonstrated. CES findings are preliminary: evidence from the small trials suggests improvement of selected objective sleep parameters, but the evidence base is limited to two small studies, one of which lacked a sham condition. In conclusion, non-invasive neuromodulation methods, specifically tDCS and CES, may impact athletic performance and help treat sleep disorders in athletes. Neuromodulation should not be viewed as a standalone method, but rather a complementary tool to other known interventions for insomnia in athletes. Although the aforementioned techniques show promising results, the research on this topic is limited and requires further evaluation.

papers.title: Patch-seq analysis reveals transcriptomic correlates of neuronal firing rate adaptation across subtypes and species.
papers.abstract: Can the transcriptomic profile of a neuron predict its physiological properties? Using a Patch-seq dataset of the primary visual cortex, we addressed this question by focusing on spike rate adaptation (SRA), a well-known phenomenon that depends on small conductance calcium (Ca)-dependent potassium (SK) channels. We first show that in parvalbumin-expressing (PV) and somatostatin-expressing (SST) interneurons, expression levels of genes encoding the ion channels underlying action potential generation are correlated with the half-width (HW) of spikes. Surprisingly, the SK encoding genes are not correlated with the degree of SRA (dAdap). Instead, genes that encode proteins upstream from the SK current, as well as the low-voltage-activated calcium channel, are correlated with dAdap. This general principle is supported by datasets from the mouse primary motor cortex and multiple macaque brain regions. Finally, we generate testable predictions by constructing a minimal computational model.

papers.title: Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common complication after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. This study aimed to evaluate whether a subanesthetic dose of esketamine reduces the incidence of PSD. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 196 women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Participants were randomly assigned to the esketamine or control group. During anesthesia induction, the esketamine group received an intravenous bolus of esketamine 0.2 mg/kg, whereas the control group received an equivalent volume of normal saline. The primary analysis was conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle, with missing outcome data handled using multiple imputation; 189 participants (95 in the control group and 94 in the esketamine group) were included in the per-protocol sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was the incidence of PSD on postoperative day (POD) 3, defined using a composite criterion of an Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) score ≥6 or a numerical rating scale (NRS) score ≥6. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of PSD on POD 1, postoperative pain scores, postoperative anxiety and depression scores, and patient satisfaction with the anesthetic technique. In the intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation, the estimated incidence of PSD on POD 3 was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (13.06% vs 24.90%; risk difference, -11.84 percentage points [95% CI, -22.98 to -0.69]; relative risk [RR], 0.52 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.047). The per-protocol (PP) sensitivity analysis yielded similar results (12.8% vs 24.2%; RR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.043). PSD on POD 1 did not differ between the groups. No between-group differences in postoperative anxiety or depression scores were noted. Postoperative pain scores at 30 minutes were significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.001). Dreaming was more frequent in the esketamine group (21.4% vs 11.2%; P = 0.048), and the time to full alertness (12 [10-14] vs 11 [9-13] minutes; P = 0.002) and postanesthesia care unit (PACU) stay (34 [30-37] vs 31 [29-34] minutes; P = 0.005) were modestly longer. A single subanesthetic dose of esketamine was associated with a lower incidence of short-term PSD on POD 3 in women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings. China Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2500105998.

papers.title: Sleep Stage Classification Across Heterogeneous EEG/EOG Channels with Multi-channel Differential Transformer.
papers.abstract: Classification of sleep stages is essential for assessing sleep quality and diagnosing sleep disorders. However, manual inspection of EEG characteristics for each stage is time-consuming and prone to human error. Although machine learning and deep learning methods have been actively developed, they continue to face challenges arising from the non-stationarity and variability of electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) signals across diverse clinical configurations, often resulting in poor generalization. In this work, we propose SleepDIFFormer, a multi-channel differential transformer framework for heterogeneous EEG-EOG representation learning. SleepDIFFormer is trained across multiple sleep staging datasets, each treated as a source domain, with the goal of generalizing to unseen target domains. Specifically, it employs a Multi-channel Differential Transformer Architecture (MDTA) designed to process raw EEG and EOG signals while incorporating cross-domain alignment. Our approach mitigates spatial and temporal attention noise and learns a domain-invariant EEG-EOG representation through feature distribution alignment across datasets, thereby enhancing generalization to new domains. Empirically, we evaluated SleepDIFFormer on five diverse sleep staging datasets under domain generalization settings and benchmarked it against existing approaches, achieving superior performance. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation analyses and interpretation of the differential attention weights demonstrated their relevance to learning discriminative sleep EEG representations. These findings support the development of more generalizable approaches to automated sleep-stage classification. Our source code and checkpoint are made publicly available at https://github.com/Ben1001409/SleepDIFFormer.

papers.title: Early Postoperative Psychological Resilience Patterns and Associated Factors in Patients with Knee Stiffness Undergoing Arthroscopic Release Surgery: A Latent Class Growth Model Study.
papers.abstract: Knee stiffness substantially impairs mobility and quality of life. Although arthroscopic release can improve joint function, little is known about early postoperative changes in psychological resilience among these patients. This study aimed to identify heterogeneous early postoperative psychological resilience patterns in patients with knee stiffness undergoing arthroscopic release surgery and to explore factors associated with pattern membership. A prospective observational study was conducted among patients undergoing arthroscopic release for knee stiffness. Psychological resilience was assessed using the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale at four time points: admission before surgery, 3 days after surgery, 2 weeks after surgery, and 1 month after surgery. Latent class growth modeling was used to identify early postoperative resilience pattern groups. Univariate analyses and multinomial logistic regression were conducted to explore factors associated with pattern membership. Multicollinearity among candidate predictors was assessed before multivariable modeling. A total of 240 patients completed all four assessments. The LCGM identified three early postoperative psychological resilience pattern groups: the Low Resilience Declining Group (17.1%), the Moderate Resilience Stable Group (68.8%), and the High Resilience Increasing Group (14.2%). Multinomial logistic regression using standardized continuous psychosocial predictors showed that, compared with the High Resilience Increasing Group, patients in the Low Resilience Declining Group had lower perceived social support and poorer sleep quality. Compared with the High Resilience Increasing Group, patients in the Moderate Resilience Stable Group were more likely to have a primary-school education or below, lower perceived social support, and lower ERRI scores. Psychological resilience showed heterogeneous patterns during the early postoperative period after arthroscopic release for knee stiffness. The findings may help identify patients who are psychologically vulnerable during early recovery, but should be interpreted as exploratory because of the single-center design, short follow-up duration, and limited subgroup sizes. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up and orthopedic outcome measures are needed to validate these early postoperative patterns and clarify their clinical significance. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01903-1.

papers.title: Timing the effort: Chronobiological drivers of skeletal muscle adaptation and metabolic health.
papers.abstract: Exercise acts as a non-photic zeitgeber, resetting skeletal muscle circadian clocks that regulate metabolism, mitochondrial function, and insulin sensitivity. This review synthesizes current evidence on how exercise timing modulates skeletal muscle clock function and metabolic adaptation, with emphasis on divergent molecular pathways, sex-specific regulation, chrono-nutrition, and emerging evidence on immune-circadian interactions, myokine-mediated muscle-organ communication, and cellular stress responses. Exercise performed at different circadian phases activates distinct signaling networks despite identical mechanical workloads. Early active phase exercise, typically performed following an overnight fast, preferentially activates the AMPK-SIRT1-HIF1α axis, promoting lipid oxidation, metabolic stress sensing, and circadian phase advancement through PER/CRY modulation. Conversely, late phase exercise favors p38 MAPK-ATF2/CREB-PGC-1α signaling, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and Akt-AS160-GLUT4-mediated glucose disposal. Emerging evidence further suggests that circadian regulation of macrophage polarization, cGAS-STING signaling, contraction-induced myokine secretion, and proteostasis may contribute to time-dependent systemic adaptations, although direct human evidence remains limited. In addition, pronounced sexual dimorphism indicates that estrogen-mediated regulation of BMAL1/CLOCK signaling influences mitochondrial function and substrate selection. In conclusion, exercise timing represents an important regulator of metabolic health. Integrating circadian biology, nutritional timing, chronotype, sex, metabolic phenotype, and immune-metabolic context may facilitate the development of precision chrono-exercise strategies for metabolic and cardiometabolic disorders.

papers.title: Composite sleep patterns and the allergy-related composite outcome among American and Chinese older adults: exploration of depressive symptoms as a potential mediator.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms commonly co-occur in older adults, but their associations with heterogeneous allergy-related outcomes and the role of depressive symptoms remain unclear. We analyzed 1,562 participants aged ≥60 years from NHANES 2005-2006. A composite sleep pattern combined sleep duration, trouble sleeping, and diagnosed sleep disorders. The allergy-related composite outcome comprised elevated total immunoglobulin E and seven questionnaire-assessed disease or symptom outcomes. Survey-weighted logistic regression evaluated associations. Depressive symptoms were assessed with a modified 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8), and statistical mediation examined indirect associations through its continuous score. We also conducted a complementary longitudinal analysis in 6,146 Chinese older adults from CHARLS. Poor versus healthy sleep was associated with higher odds of the allergy-related composite outcome (OR 2.100; 95% CI 1.328-3.322), wheeze (OR 2.148; 95% CI 1.296-3.559), and sneeze (OR 1.636; 95% CI 1.135-2.357). The estimated indirect association through depressive symptoms represented 22.5% of the total association. In CHARLS, impaired sleep quality was associated with incident asthma (OR 1.689; 95% CI 1.254-2.275), and the corresponding indirect association through depressive symptoms represented 28.3% of the total association. Poor sleep was associated with heterogeneous allergy-related outcomes among US older adults, while CHARLS provided complementary longitudinal evidence for incident asthma. Depressive symptoms statistically accounted for part of the observed sleep-allergy association.
papers.journal: The Journal of asthma : official journal of the Association for the Care of Asthma

papers.title: Baduanjin Exercise Across Clinical Conditions: An Umbrella Review.
papers.abstract: Baduanjin (BDJ) is a traditional Chinese mind-body exercise increasingly evaluated in rehabilitation and chronic disease care. The growth of systematic reviews has made the literature difficult to interpret because review volume, methodological quality, certainty of evidence, and overlap of primary trials are rarely considered together. This umbrella review aimed to map the clinical condition spectrum of BDJ research and to appraise the credibility and redundancy of the existing review evidence. Eight English and Chinese databases were searched from inception to April 2026 for systematic reviews and meta-analyses in which BDJ was a standalone or separable intervention. Eligible reviews were mapped by clinical condition. Representative core reviews were selected using prespecified hierarchical criteria. Methodological quality, certainty of evidence, and primary-trial overlap were assessed using A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews 2 (AMSTAR 2), grading of recommendations assessment, development and evaluation (GRADE), and corrected covered area (CCA), respectively. A total of 261 reviews were included. Thirty-one core reviews underwent AMSTAR 2 appraisal, 21 condition-outcome pairs underwent GRADE assessment, and 10 review clusters underwent CCA analysis. Review activity was concentrated in cardiovascular/cardiac rehabilitation, musculoskeletal pain, cognitive/neurological rehabilitation, endocrine/metabolic disorders, psychological/sleep/emotional conditions, oncology/postoperative rehabilitation, and respiratory disease. AMSTAR 2 ratings were moderate in one review, low in 18, and critically low in 12. Nineteen condition-outcome pairs were rated low certainty and 2 very low certainty. Several clusters showed high or very high primary-trial overlap. BDJ has been reviewed widely, but the evidence is methodologically uneven, frequently overlapping, and of low or very low certainty. Current findings should be interpreted as uncertain evidence signals rather than practice recommendations.

papers.title: End-of-life experiences: a multicenter longitudinal study on characteristics and prevalence in terminally ill patients.
papers.abstract: Evidence suggests that transcendent end-of-life experiences (ELEs) are common and impact the dying; however, there is a shortage of longitudinal studies. To evaluate the prevalence and characteristics of ELEs in terminally ill patients. This multicenter longitudinal mixed‑methods study collected demographic, clinical, and ELE‑related data-including prevalence, content, and comfort/distress ratings-from patients with a Palliative Performance Scale (PPS) ≤ 50% across three palliative care units in Brazil. Data were gathered through repeated interviews until death, discharge, or ongoing hospitalization by the study's end. Descriptive statistics were performed. Among 85 patients, 52% were female (44) and mean age was 61 (range 28-93); religiosity/spirituality was common (63% moderately/very religious, 98% believed in God, 65% in afterlife). Functional status declined progressively during follow‑up, with mean PPS decreasing from approximately 40 early in observation to 10 near death. ELEs were reported across varying levels of impairment. Of these patients, 34% experienced ELEs, with a median interval of 29.5 days from the first ELE to death (range: 1-186 days). Nearly half of the ELEs (49%) occurred during sleep, and 80% were perceived as real. The majority of ELEs involved deceased loved ones (52%), with 36% being described as comforting and 27% as distressing. Additionally, 78% of ELEs were reported by non-delirious patients. ELEs exhibited consistent patterns in timing, phenomenology, and content, supporting the possibility that they represent an inherent feature of the dying process. Cultural and psychosocial contexts may shape both the interpretation of ELEs and their emotional valence.

papers.title: A hypothalamic circuit links high-fat diet exposure to anxiety-like behavior and anxiety-associated hyperphagia.
papers.abstract: Obesity and anxiety disorders are frequently comorbid, yet the neural circuit mechanisms linking metabolic and affective states remain incompletely understood. Here, in male mice exposed to long-term high-fat diet, we identify a hypothalamic circuit comprising arcuate nucleus agouti-related protein neurons and paraventricular nucleus corticotropin-releasing hormone neurons that regulates anxiety-like behavior under metabolic stress, with downstream recruitment of lateral hypothalamic area glutamatergic neurons to modulate feeding in a state-dependent manner. In vivo fiber photometry and ex vivo electrophysiology show that high-fat diet enhances activity and feeding-locked recruitment of this circuit, associated with increased anxiety-like behavior and feeding. Circuit-specific inhibition attenuates both phenotypes, whereas corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 2 signaling in the lateral hypothalamic area selectively mediates high-fat diet-associated hyperphagia without affecting anxiety-like behavior. In this work, we show a disease-state-dependent hypothalamic circuit differentially recruited under chronic high-fat diet to coordinate anxiety-related behavior and feeding output, providing a framework for metabolic-affective interactions.

papers.title: [The association between circadian rhythm disruption-related behaviors and myopia in children and adolescents].
papers.abstract: Child and adolescent myopia has become a critical global public health concern, with its prevalence steadily rising worldwide. Shifts in circadian behaviors, including irregular sleep schedules and increased nighttime exposure to artificial light, have contributed to widespread circadian rhythm disruptions manifested as sleep disorders, social jetlag, and excessive nighttime blue light exposure. Accumulating evidence suggests that circadian rhythm-disrupting behaviors are closely linked to the onset and progression of myopia in children and adolescents, although the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper systematically reviews the associations between circadian rhythm-disrupting behaviors and pediatric and adolescent myopia, as well as the potential pathogenic mechanisms involved. It further summarizes existing myopia intervention strategies targeting circadian behavioral abnormalities. By optimizing circadian behavioral patterns, this review aims to provide novel insights and evidence for the precise prevention and control of childhood and adolescent myopia.

papers.title: [Association of beverage consumption patterns with different types of obesity among children and adolescents in Renhuai City, Guizhou Province].
papers.abstract: Objective: To investigate the associations between different beverage consumption patterns and general obesity, abdominal obesity, and their coexistence in children and adolescents, and to analyze the differences across gender, age groups, and residential areas, so as to provide scientific evidence for precise prevention and control of childhood obesity. Methods: This was a cross-sectional study conducted in Renhuai City, Guizhou Province, involving 11 646 children and adolescents. Principal component analysis was employed to extract beverage consumption patterns. General obesity (BMI ≥95th percentile for age and sex) and abdominal obesity (waist circumference ≥90th percentile for age and sex) were defined according to the Screening for Overweight and Obesity in School-age Children and Adolescents (WS/T 586-2018) and the Screening Thresholds for High Waist Circumference in Children and Adolescents Aged 7-18 Years (WS/T 611-2018), respectively. Multivariate logistic regression was used to analyze the associations between beverage patterns and three types of obesity (general obesity, abdominal obesity, and their coexistence), with subgroup analyses stratified by gender, age group, and residential area. Results: Among 11 646 children and adolescents, two beverage patterns were extracted, named the carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage group and the dairy-juice group. Analysis of population distribution characteristics showed that the carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage group had a higher proportion of males (χ²=32.327, P<0.001), adolescents (χ²=110.242, P<0.001), boarders (χ²=18.053, P<0.001), and urban residents (χ²=83.999, P<0.001). Regarding lifestyle factors, the carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage group had a higher proportion of individuals who did not meet the screen time recommendation (χ²=22.955, P<0.001) and did not meet the moderate-to-vigorous physical activity recommendation (χ²=6.622, P=0.010). The Food Diversity Score[M(Q1, Q3)] for the carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage group was 3(1, 6), while that for the dairy-juice group was 4 (2, 7) (Z=-12.233, P<0.001). Sleep duration[M(Q1, Q3)] for the carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage group was 8.5 (7.5, 9.3) h/d, whereas for the dairy-juice group it was 8.9 (8.1, 9.5) h/d (Z=-10.505, P<0.001). Both the Food Diversity Score and sleep duration were lower in the carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage group than in the dairy-juice group. Multivariate logistic regression showed that, using the dairy-juice group as the reference, the carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage group was positively associated with general obesity (OR=1.154, 95%CI: 1.021-1.304, P=0.021), abdominal obesity (OR=1.195, 95%CI: 1.078-1.324, P<0.001), and the coexistence of both obesity types (OR=1.175, 95%CI: 1.024-1.347, P=0.021). These associations remained significant after correction using the MEff method (α=0.022). In subgroup analyses, the carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage group was positively associated with the three obesity phenotypes in adolescents (P<0.01), with abdominal obesity in males (OR=1.224, 95%CI: 1.083-1.383, P=0.001), and with abdominal obesity in urban students (OR=1.163, 95%CI: 1.041-1.298, P=0.007). These associations also remained significant after correction using the MEff method. Conclusions: The carbonated-stimulant-sweetener beverage pattern was significantly positively associated with all obesity indicators in children and adolescents. Further subgroup analyses showed that these positive associations were more pronounced among adolescents, males, and urban residents.

papers.title: Dysregulation of Orexin-A and Implications for Renal Function Assessment in Chronic Kidney Disease.
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a long-standing kidney condition in which the kidneys are gradually damaged. It usually has multiple symptoms and is often accompanied by complications, such as hormonal imbalances, high blood pressure, anemia, and sleep disorders. Orexin, occasionally mentioned as hypocretin, is a neuropeptide that is mostly generated by orexin-containing neurons in the hypothalamus. Their receptors are found in a variety of tissues, such as the brain and kidney. This study aims to evaluate the impact of renal function on orexin-A levels in CKD. The study included 44 adult patients diagnosed with CKD, and their results were compared with 44 healthy participants of the same age and sex. An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kit was used to measure orexin-A, while urea, creatinine, and lipid profile were measured using spectrophotometric methods. Association with orexin-A was performed using Pearson's correlation analysis. The results showed a significant decrease in serum orexin-A (P < 0.001) in patients with CKD. Correlation analysis showed that orexin-A in CKD patients was positively correlated with serum creatinine (r = 0.353, P = 0.018) and high-density lipoprotein (r = 0.354, P = 0.017), while negatively correlated with glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (r = -0.424, P = 0.004). Orexin-A levels decreased in patients with CKD, and this decrease reflects the disruption of the orexin system, which was inversely related to the GFR and directly related to creatinine and high-density lipoprotein levels.

papers.title: A Call to Action: Challenges and Future Directions for Sleep Health in Europe.
papers.abstract: Sleep is fundamental to physical, cognitive, and emotional health and wellbeing. However, it is increasingly threatened by environmental, social, technological, and cultural pressures. To identify key priorities for improving sleep health across Europe, the European Sleep Research Society (ESRS)'s Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Committee (EDIC) and Early Career Network (ECN) convened a joint taskforce to review current challenges and develop strategic recommendations. Through a scoping review of the literature, iterative consensus meetings, and collaborative synthesis, the taskforce identified five overarching challenges: (1) environmental and climate-related threats to sleep; (2) inequitable access to sleep medicine and care; (3) the rapid expansion and potential of digital health technologies; (4) widespread sleep misinformation and misconceptions surrounding sleep health; and (5) societal change, constant technological connectivity, and the emergence of a 24/7 culture. These interconnected challenges disproportionately affect vulnerable groups and risk exacerbating existing health inequalities. In response, we propose a coordinated set of recommendations structured according to the PESTEL framework (Political, Economic, Sociological, Technological, Environmental and Legal). Collectively, these recommendations advocate for integrated and equity-focused approaches to strengthen the structural and organisational conditions that support sleep health, improve sleep health literacy, regulate emerging technologies, and ensure that healthy sleep becomes an achievable public health priority across Europe.

papers.title: Neuro-Immune Interactions in the Tumour Microenvironment: Implications for Cancer Progression and Treatment.
papers.abstract: The nervous and immune systems, once viewed as distinct biological networks, are now understood to be closely linked in regulating cancer development, progression, and responses to therapy. Neural structures infiltrate the tumour microenvironment and communicate with immune cells, influencing key processes such as tumour growth, invasion, and metastatic spread. Through neurotransmitters, neuropeptides, and continuous signalling between peripheral tissues and the brain, nerves affect immune cell recruitment, activity, and overall immune balance. Factors including psychological stress, circadian rhythm disturbances, and gut-brain communication further shape antitumour immune responses, highlighting the complexity of these interactions. Research suggests that neuronal signalling not only contributes to cancer-associated symptoms, such as pain, but also affects the efficacy of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. Neural biomarkers may provide prognostic value, while interventions targeting neural pathways could strengthen anticancer immunity. Nevertheless, major challenges remain, including cellular heterogeneity, dynamic spatial and temporal interactions, and the limitations of existing experimental models. Continued progress in molecular techniques, bioinformatics, and cross-disciplinary research will be crucial for clarifying these mechanisms. Investigating the neuro-immune-cancer interface offers significant potential for developing innovative treatment approaches that combine neuroscience, immunology, and oncology to enhance patient survival and quality of life.

Zona incerta circuits in cognition and the regulation of sleep and wakefulness: potential relevance to Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive decline and prominent disturbances in sleep and wakefulness, reflecting dysfunction across distributed neural networks. The zona incerta (ZI) is a highly heterogeneous subthalamic structure whose organization is defined by spatial location, molecular identity, neurochemical phenotype, and circuit connectivity. Recent studies demonstrate that distinct ZI cell populations and projections contribute to memory processing, novelty seeking, cortical plasticity, sleep promotion, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, transitions to wakefulness, and sleep homeostasis. Together, these findings suggest that the ZI is better viewed as a state-dependent subcortical regulatory platform than as a unitary cognitive or sleep center. Emerging pathological evidence further raises the possibility that the ZI may be relevant to neurodegeneration. Amyloid-β deposition has been reported in the ZI of 5xFAD transgenic mice, while experimental tau propagation, human tauopathies other than AD, and studies of other neurodegenerative disorders indicate potential cellular and circuit vulnerability. However, direct evidence from human AD remains lacking, and no study has established a causal pathway from AD pathology to selective ZI dysfunction and subsequent cognitive or sleep impairment. We therefore propose two testable models in which the ZI contributes to AD phenotypes either as a shared circuit node or through parallel, selectively vulnerable functional modules.

papers.title: Should I "stay" or should I "go"? Influence of an anticipated stop on cortical correlates of overground walking.
papers.abstract: Real-world walking frequently requires pedestrians to maintain proactive inhibition to safely navigate unpredictable environments. While cortical modulations occurring during locomotion under environmental uncertainty are well-established, the specific proactive mechanisms underlying this state of inhibitory anticipation remain unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the behavioral and cortical shifts associated with anticipating a stop during overground walking. Fourteen healthy young adults performed fluent and cautious walking tasks with an expected stop. Cortical activity and trunk acceleration were recorded using a 32-channel mobile electroencephalography and an integrated accelerometer. Step-1 latency and step-interval variability were calculated via heel strike detection. Gait-phase-related power modulations were computed, and spectral principal component analysis was applied to attenuate artifacts. The results revealed that cautious walking significantly increased step-interval variability, whereas step-1 latency remained unaffected. At the cortical level, left frontotemporal areas exhibited an attenuated and delayed theta desynchronization during the swing phase. Furthermore, centroparietal regions demonstrated an altered temporal profile of alpha and beta synchronization, characterized by enhanced late-stance synchronization and reduced swing-phase synchronization. The present findings suggest that anticipating a potential stop may alter the rhythmic consistency of gait and reorganize phase-specific cortical dynamics. Being prepared to stop may shift the neural control of automated locomotion toward active monitoring, highlighting the relevance of proactive inhibition during everyday mobility.

papers.title: Differing subjective and psychophysiological response patterns to a music-based auditory intervention for anxiety.
papers.abstract: Anxiety comprises partially dissociable cognitive and somatic components, yet it remains unclear whether brief interventions modulate these systems in parallel. This randomized controlled trial examined subjective and psychophysiological responses to a brief music-based auditory intervention relative to an active auditory control (pink noise) in undergraduate students reporting recent generalized anxiety symptoms. Participants (N = 83) were randomized to the auditory intervention or pink noise. Cognitive and somatic anxiety were assessed before and after the intervention, while salivary cortisol, heart rate variability (HRV), and electroencephalography (EEG) indexed endocrine, autonomic, and neural processes. Cortisol showed a significant Condition × Time interaction, with larger reductions following the auditory intervention. Midline theta power also exhibited a significant Condition × Time interaction, reflecting opposing patterns of change across conditions, although within-condition changes were only significant in the pink noise condition. Cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety, affective arousal, frontal alpha lateralization, and HRV did not show significant differential baseline-to-post change. During listening, HRV increased across conditions, but the Condition × Epoch interaction observed in the primary growth model was not retained when participant-specific slopes were included. Together, these findings indicate differing patterns of response across levels of analysis, with broad reductions in self-reported anxiety and arousal across both auditory conditions and greater condition sensitivity in the primary cortisol and midline-theta analyses. Because the cortisol and theta interactions were not retained in models including all physiologically valid observations, these condition-dependent findings should be interpreted cautiously.

papers.title: Prevalence, risk factors, and lived experiences of insomnia among cancer caregivers: A mixed-method study.
papers.abstract: Insomnia affects 40-76% of cancer caregivers, yet prevalence estimates vary widely and evidence on associated factors and lived experiences remains limited. Guided by the 3P model of insomnia, this study estimated insomnia prevalence, identified associated factors, and explored caregivers' lived experiences and treatment preferences. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study was conducted among informal cancer caregivers in China. Insomnia was assessed using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), and associated factors were examined by stepwise multivariable logistic regression. Semi-structured interviews with caregivers experiencing insomnia were analysed using qualitative content analysis. Among 427 caregivers, 52.0% reported clinically significant insomnia symptoms (ISI > 7). Predisposing factors included older age (aOR = 1.03), family history of insomnia (aOR = 3.12) and medication use for conditions other than insomnia (aOR = 0.41); higher anxiety symptoms (aOR = 1.30) were precipitating, and higher pre-sleep arousal (aOR = 1.03) perpetuating. Only 13.3% (57/427) of caregivers had ever used an insomnia intervention, and evidence-based psychological interventions were rarely used (9.4% of users). Qualitative findings showed that night-time caregiving demands, emotional distress and environmental disruptions contributed to insomnia onset and persistence, and caregivers preferred flexible, remotely delivered non-pharmacological interventions. To our knowledge, this is the first mixed-methods study in China to apply the 3P model to insomnia among cancer caregivers while also exploring their lived experiences and treatment preferences. Insomnia was highly prevalent and undertreated. Routine sleep screening and scalable, caregiver-adapted non-pharmacological interventions should be prioritised to support caregivers' sleep health and caregiving capacity.

papers.title: Sleep underestimation and subjective sleep appraisal: Limited value of routine polysomnographic and electroencephalographic features.
papers.abstract: Whether routine polysomnographic (PSG) and electroencephalographic (EEG) features distinguish patients who underestimate sleep remains unclear. We examined associations of clinical, subjective, PSG, and EEG features with sleep underestimation and tested whether EEG features added discrimination beyond a parsimonious three-predictor baseline model. We analysed 225 adults undergoing clinically indicated in-laboratory PSG in this single-centre retrospective cross-sectional study. The misperception index ([objective - subjective total sleep time]/objective total sleep time) was dichotomised at the cohort median (0.148) and analysed continuously. Group differences across 717 variables underwent Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Out-of-fold (OOF) discrimination was compared between a three-predictor baseline model (sleep quality, Epworth Sleepiness Scale score, and age) and an EEG-enhanced model; continuous-index analyses were exploratory. Fifty-six participants (24.9%) overestimated sleep. Objective total sleep time did not differ between groups, whereas self-rated sleep quality did (q = 0.002). None of 600 EEG features survived FDR correction (smallest q = 0.064). At the median threshold, OOF areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) were 0.6786 (baseline) and 0.6564 (EEG-enhanced; ΔAUC = -0.0221; paired DeLong P = 0.4483). Across 50 repeated partitions, median ΔAUC was -0.0261 for EEG features and +0.0096 for four macrostructural PSG variables. Obstructive sleep apnoea prevalence did not differ significantly between groups. Self-rated sleep quality was more consistently associated with sleep underestimation than routine PSG and EEG features. EEG features did not demonstrate incremental OOF discrimination beyond the baseline model. Subjective sleep appraisal should be assessed alongside PSG; underlying mechanisms require prospective investigation.

papers.title: Coupled cardio-pulmonary-cerebral functional dynamics for high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
papers.abstract: Cardiac arrest (CA) is one of the leading causes of death worldwide. High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can effectively improve the survival rate of CA patients. To find physiological indicators particularly those reflecting the cerebral function to assess the quality of CPR is a challenging issue. This study aimed to investigate the cardio-pulmonary-cerebral coupling to assess the physiological status of CA patients during CPR. Arterial blood pressure (ABP), electroencephalography (EEG), and end-tidal carbon dioxide partial pressure (PETCO2) signals collected in porcine experiments were divided into four periods: Baseline, CA, CPR, and recovery of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Cross recurrence quantification analysis (CRQA) was applied to examine the dynamical couplings of ABP-EEG, ABP-PETCO2, and EEG-PETCO2 during the four periods. In addition, a joint recurrence quantification analysis (JRQA) was applied to examine the cardio-pulmonary-cerebral dynamical coupling across the ABP, EEG, and PETCO2 during the four periods. The RR, DET, ENTR, and Lmax of ABP-PETCO2 coupling using CRQA were significantly lower during CA than during Baseline, and these parameters were significantly higher during CPR and ROSC than during CA. The RR and DET of ABP-EEG and PETCO2-EEG coupling were highest during CPR and lowest during CA (p < 0.05), and they were higher in the T7 cortical region during Baseline than other regions (p < 0.05). The RR, DET, and ENTR of ABP-PETCO2-EEG coupling using JRQA showed significantly higher values during CA than during the other periods, and the Lmax of ABP-PETCO2-EEG coupling exhibited significantly lower values during CA than during the other periods. Dynamical coupling of ABP-PETCO2-EEG could reflect the physiological states of CA patients. The T7 cortical region was identified as the most sensitive to the CPR process. This study sheds light on the value of cardio-pulmonary-cerebral dynamical coupling in indication of the effects of CPR and may play a role in screening the function of vital organs during emergency treatment.

papers.title: Physical activity and sleep patterns in women 1 year after gestational diabetes: Results from the Face-it study.
papers.abstract: Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and adequate, high-quality sleep are important for cardiometabolic health in women with recent gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) but are likely reduced during early motherhood. These behaviours may be associated; however, device-measured sleep data and studies of these associations remain scarce in this population. This cross sectional study characterised MVPA and sleep patterns and examined their associations in women with recent GDM. In the Face-it trial, 185 women provided device-measured MVPA and sleep data 1 year after delivery. Sleep variables included duration and efficiency, reflecting sleep quantity and quality. Duration was categorised as <6, 6-8 (reference) and >8 h/night. Associations with MVPA were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with site as a random intercept, adjusted for potential confounders. Two-thirds (61.6%) met WHO recommendations for moderate-intensity physical activity (PA), whereas few (3.2%) met recommendations for vigorous-intensity PA. Most met recommendations for sleep duration (87.6%) and sleep efficiency (83.8%). Compared to 6-8 h/night, there was no difference in MVPA among those sleeping <6 h/night (β = -2.5, 95% CI = -11.8, 6.7, p = 0.593). Durations >8 h/night were associated with less MVPA (β = -13.5, 95% CI = -23.0, -4.0, p = 0.006). Sleep efficiency was positively associated with MVPA (β = 0.6, 95% CI = 0.1, 1.1, p = 0.018). The association between high-quality sleep and greater MVPA suggests that PA and sleep may not only independently be relevant to cardiometabolic health but may also be associated in women with recent GDM.

papers.title: Associations Between Temporomandibular Disorder-Related Symptoms, Psychological Distress, and Sleep Quality Among Hospital Healthcare Staff.
papers.abstract: To examine associations between temporomandibular disorder (TMD)-related symptoms, psychological distress, and sleep quality among hospital healthcare staff, and to explore whether cumulative psychological-sleep burden was associated with pain-related TMD in a graded pattern. This cross-sectional study included 193 healthcare employees from a tertiary public hospital in Beijing, China. TMD-related symptoms were assessed using self-reported symptom items from the Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders (DC/TMD) Symptom Questionnaire for symptom screening rather than definitive clinical diagnosis. Psychological distress was measured using the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21 (DASS-21), and sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). An exploratory psychological-sleep composite burden index was constructed by summing standardized depression, anxiety, stress, and global PSQI scores. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated associations between the composite index and pain-related TMD, adjusting for age group, sex, and occupational role. Quartile-based trend and sensitivity analyses were performed. Pain-related TMD was reported by 67 participants (34.7%). Each 1-SD increase in the composite index showed a positive but borderline association with pain-related TMD (adjusted OR = 1.36, 95% CI: 1.00-1.86, p = 0.052). In quartile-based analysis, each higher burden quartile was associated with increased odds of pain-related TMD (adjusted OR = 1.37, 95% CI: 1.03-1.81, p = 0.030). After excluding headache-only cases, the quartile-based association remained significant (adjusted OR = 1.37, 95% CI: 1.02-1.85, p = 0.037). Symptom-specific analyses showed heterogeneous patterns. Higher cumulative psychological-sleep burden was associated with greater odds of pain-related TMD among hospital healthcare staff, particularly in quartile-based analyses. These findings support a cautious biopsychosocial interpretation and suggest that psychological distress and sleep quality may be relevant considerations in occupational oral health assessment.

papers.title: Environmental Exposures, Chronic Sinusitis, and Olfaction in People With Cystic Fibrosis.
papers.abstract: Environmental air pollutants may contribute to chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS), but their relationship with upper airway disease in people with cystic fibrosis (CF) remains poorly understood. This study evaluated associations between long-term ambient air pollutant exposure and CRS severity and olfactory dysfunction in adults with CF and CRS. 80 adults with CF and comorbid CRS were prospectively enrolled from 2019 to 2023 at multiple U.S. academic rhinology centers. Long-term exposure to PM2.5, PM10, CO, SO2, NO2, and ozone was estimated using the nearest U.S. Environmental Protection Agency monitor linked to each participant's residential ZIP code, with 3-year mean exposure calculated before enrollment. CRS severity and olfaction were assessed using Lund-Kennedy endoscopy scores, Lund-Mackay CT scores, SNOT-22, Questionnaire of Olfactory Disorders-Negative Statements, and 40-item Smell Identification Test. Analyses used Spearman correlations and nonparametric group comparisons. Higher ozone exposure was associated with worse total SNOT-22 scores (Rs = 0.34 p = 0.002), including ear/facial, psychological, and sleep dysfunction domains, as well as worse olfactory-specific outcomes, including higher QOD-NS scores (Rs = 0.30, p = 0.007) and lower Smell Identification Test scores (Rs = -0.30, p = 0.018). Other pollutants did not show significant associations with CRS or olfactory outcomes. In adults with CF and CRS, higher long-term ambient ozone exposure was associated with greater sinonasal symptom burden and worse olfactory function. These findings suggest that ozone may be an environmental contributor to upper airway disease severity in this population and support further study in larger, adjusted analyses. Increased ozone pollution correlates with more severe CRS in people with CF. Among people with CF and CRS, higher ozone exposure is associated with worse olfactory function.

papers.title: Ayurveda in Integrative Oncology: Aligning Traditional Principles with Conventional Cancer Care.
papers.abstract: Patients challenged with cancer diagnosis and treatments often seek solutions beyond conventional therapies to improve their quality of life and immunity and to manage symptoms, concerns, coping, and daily functioning. Ayurveda, a traditional medical system originating in India, has generated growing interest within integrative oncology; however, limited clarity and evidence exist regarding its appropriate application and integration across the oncology care continuum. This paper explores the evolving landscape of integrative oncology, focusing on the incorporation of Ayurveda into global cancer care. With emphasis on evidence-based practices, we discuss the similarities and distinctions between Ayurvedic and integrative oncology approaches including nutrition, exercise, mind body practices, sleep, and use of herbal supplements. We aim to stimulate further dialogue and multidisciplinary collaboration between oncology healthcare providers and Ayurveda clinicians. Developing a patient-centered, evidence-informed, integrative model of care that incorporates Ayurvedic approaches has the potential to enhance the quality of life for patients along the cancer trajectory. This discussion may stimulate further research and medical education with the goal of incorporating supported Ayurvedic approaches into mainstream cancer care.

papers.title: Optogenetic cardioversion: To depolarize or to hyperpolarize?
Contextual Stress Exposure and Longitudinal Change in Mental Health and Sleep Among US Latino/a Adolescents.
papers.abstract: This research examines how contextual stress exposure within the immigration environment predicts sleep problems and internalizing symptoms for Latino/a adolescents. Participants included N = 547 adolescents listed as "Hispanic" on 2017-18 middle school enrollment lists in a suburban Atlanta, GA, school district. Using three time (T) points of survey data (2021-23), structural equation models tested paths from immigration-related stressors to changes in sleep problems and internalizing symptoms. Missing data were addressed using multiply imputed datasets and full information maximum likelihood. At T1, the 244 (44.6%) male and 303 (55.4%) female participants had a mean (SD) age of 16.2 (.91) years. Across time, 28.8%-40.3% of youth reported <7 hours of sleep on average. The prevalence of clinical internalizing symptoms ranged from 31.1% to 35.9% for female participants and from 29.9% to 44.3% for male participants. T1 immigration-related stressors predicted T1 to T2 increases in sleep problems (ß = .12 [95% CI = .03-.20]) and internalizing symptoms (ß = .09 [95% CI = .01-.17]). T2 sleep problems mediated associations between T1 immigration-related stressors and T2 to T3 increases in internalizing symptoms (indirect effect: ß = .01 [95% CI = .00-.03]) and sleep problems (indirect effect: ß = .07 [95% CI = .02-.12]). Sleep problems and internalizing symptoms were reciprocally associated from T1 to T2 (sleep to internalizing: ß = .11 [95% CI = .02-.20]; internalizing to sleep: ß = .14 [95% CI = .04-.25]) and from T2 to T3 (sleep to internalizing: ß = .11 [95% CI = .03-.20]; internalizing to sleep: ß = .10 [95% CI = .00-.20]). For Latino/a adolescents, immigration-related stressors may harm mental health through increased sleep problems.

papers.title: Predictors of Aggression in Children and Adolescents With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Aggression is a common and impairing co-occurring behavior among children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), negatively affecting developmental outcomes, family functioning, and social participation. Although numerous studies have examined factors associated with aggression in ASD, findings remain inconsistent, limiting efforts to improve early identification and intervention. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on predictors of aggression in children and adolescents with ASD. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023416081). A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was conducted from database inception to 4 April 2024. Eligible studies were evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for cross-sectional designs and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies, and findings were narratively synthesized. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria and were of generally satisfactory methodological quality. Across studies, six categories of predictors were identified: demographic, caregiver, core symptom, comorbidity, psychological, and biological factors. Social communication deficits and poor sleep quality showed relatively consistent associations with aggression, although these findings were based on only three and two studies, respectively, whereas evidence for other factors-including age, IQ, caregiver characteristics, and sensory or biological markers-was mixed. Overall, aggression in ASD appears to arise from interacting individual, familial, and contextual influences. These findings highlight the importance of assessing communication skills and sleep problems when evaluating aggression risk and suggest that interventions targeting these domains may reduce aggressive behavior. Future research should employ longitudinal and cross-cultural designs to clarify developmental pathways and strengthen the evidence base for personalized intervention strategies.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Integrated Chinese and Western Medicine for Depression With Anxiety and Somatic Symptoms: A Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveSomatic symptoms are often linked with depression and anxiety, making diagnosis difficult and limiting treatment effectiveness. Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine has been studied as a complementary approach; however, its efficacy and safety have not been systematically evaluated. This review and meta-analysis examined the effectiveness and safety of integrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine in patients diagnosed with depression with or without comorbid anxiety and somatic symptoms.MethodsThis systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. English-language studies published from 2014 to 2026 were searched in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. Randomized controlled trials comparing integrated therapy with control interventions were included. The primary outcome was depression severity assessed by HAMD scores. Secondary outcomes included anxiety symptoms, somatic symptoms, and adverse events. A random-effects model was used, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic.ResultsEleven studies met review criteria. Integrated therapy significantly reduced depression severity compared with the standard Western medicine control condition (MD = -3.95, 95% CI: -4.71 to -3.19; I2 = 59%). Anxiety symptoms were also significantly reduced (MD = -3.95, 95% CI: -4.65 to -3.26; I2 = 50%). Somatic symptoms, including sleep disturbances and pain-related outcomes, improved but were assessed descriptively because of reporting variability. Adverse events were lower or similar in combined treatment groups, indicating a favorable safety profile. Funnel plot analysis suggested minimal publication bias.ConclusionIntegrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine was associated with greater improvements in depression and anxiety symptoms than the included control interventions, which comprised Western medicine alone, placebo/sham interventions, or usual care, while showing generally good tolerability. However, given the methodological limitations, heterogeneity of comparator conditions, and low certainty of the available evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.
