papers.title: A self-organized QTPat-based feature-engineering framework for subject-independent classification of English- and Turkish-associated EEG signals.
papers.abstract: Our primary aim is to develop an automated feature-engineering framework for subject-independent classification of EEG recordings acquired from English-speaking and Turkish-speaking participant cohorts. Drawing inspiration from a quantum tunnel pattern called QTPat, we introduced a novel approach of dynamically generating directed graphs to extract textural features. For our experiments, we utilized an EEG dataset containing 1652 English sentence-EEG pairs and 1600 Turkish sentence-EEG pairs. These signals were recorded from 20 English-speaking and 20 Turkish subjects who were presented with standardized sentences in their respective native languages. During the experiments, the participants were instructed to carefully contemplate each sentence while wearing a mobile brain cap system that acquired 14-channel EEG signals. Our preprocessing pipeline involved subjecting the EEG signals to multiple filtered wavelet packet decompositions, using both 6 Daubechies and 6 symlet wavelet filters. Subsequently, we extracted textural and statistical features employing the QTPat model, along with 20 statistical moments. To enhance discriminative power, we applied neighborhood component analysis and the Chi2-function to select the most relevant features. The k-nearest neighbor classifier was then employed to calculate predictive vectors. To further refine the results, we introduced an iterative hard majority voting scheme, generating additional voted vectors. Finally, we utilized a greedy algorithm to select the best-channel-wise and overall model results. Using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO CV), the proposed framework achieved 96.37% classification accuracy using four selected EEG channels. These findings demonstrate that the QTPat-based architecture can discriminate the two language-associated EEG cohorts under subject-independent evaluation. However, because language and participant population are coupled in the available dataset, the present results should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of language-specific neural decoding. Further studies using within-subject bilingual experimental designs are required to determine whether the identified EEG patterns specifically reflect language-related neural processing.

papers.title: The impact of creatine on brain functions.
papers.abstract: As an endogenous compound essential for energy homeostasis, creatine holds a fundamental role in the bioenergetics of the brain, an organ with high metabolic requirements. This review provides a synthesis of current knowledge on the impact of creatine on the functions of the central nervous system (CNS). The brain, which is capable of de novo creatine synthesis, demonstrates an increase in its internal concentrations following supplementation; however, this effect is less significant than in muscle tissue and is constrained by the blood-brain barrier, among other factors. The development of effective CNS-targeted dosing strategies remains a subject of ongoing research. An overview of the literature suggests that creatine supplementation may beneficially influence cognitive performance, particularly under conditions of elevated metabolic demand like stress or sleep deprivation, with the potential to enhance memory and mitigate fatigue. Nonetheless, findings from the cited research are inconsistent due to methodological heterogeneity and a common failure to directly measure brain creatine levels. Reports on creatine's antidepressant properties are particularly encouraging, with preclinical and initial clinical studies pointing to its potential utility (e.g., via the mTORC1 pathway) in augmenting mood disorder treatments. Moreover, the authors examine the use of creatine in chronic fatigue syndrome, where evidence supports improvements in physical performance and reductions in pain intensity, although its effect on generalized fatigue remains ambiguous.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Yoga-based guided meditation In Improving the quality of sleep in patients with coronary artery disease: The Yoga Nidra Trial.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep quality has emerged as a risk for coronary artery disease (CAD) and is also associated with poor prognosis and increased mortality. Sleep aids, among CAD patients, lead to increased heart failure, hospitalisation, and mortality. Yoga Nidra, a form of guided meditation, has been shown to improve sleep quality and duration. The aim of the study is to evaluate the adjunctive effect of Yoga Nidra on actigraphy-measured sleep quality parameters, psychological outcomes, and health-related quality of life in patients with CAD. This is a two-arm,1:1 allocation, randomised, controlled, open-label, blinded-endpoint, single-centre trial conducted in a tertiary care hospital between 22-9-2021 and 30-03-2024.144 out of 678 consecutively screened patients with stable CAD and poor sleep quality met the eligibility criteria and were enrolled. Participants were randomised to either a 35-minute, 12-week Yoga Nidra intervention group (n = 72) or a standard care group (n = 72) with sleep hygiene counselling imparted to all patients.The primary outcome was to assess actigraphy-measured sleep efficiency. Secondary outcomes included assessments of actigraphy-derived sleep parameters, ambulatory blood pressure (BP), echocardiographic diastolic function (E/E'), psychological health, and quality-of-life evaluations using validated scales. The Yoga Nidra group exhibited significant improvements in sleep efficiency (82% [76-86] vs. 64% [57-74]; p < 0.05), total sleep time (357 ± 99 min vs. 298 ± 83 min; p < 0.05), reduced sleep latency (15 [11-24] vs. 30 [14-70] min; p < 0.05), and lower wake after sleep onset (48 [28-67] vs. 67 [37-119] min; p < 0.05). Significant improvements were also observed in perceived stress, depression levels, and quality of life. Yoga Nidra is effective in improving sleep quality inpatients with coronary artery disease.Stress, depression, and health-related quality of life also improved with Yoga Nidra.

papers.title: Cannabidiol (CBD) for Pain: A Narrative Review of Evidence to Date.
papers.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD), the principal non-intoxicating phytocannabinoid of Cannabis sativa, is widely marketed and self-administered for pain relief, yet its regulatory status as an analgesic remains unapproved. This review synthesizes preclinical mechanistic data, human pharmacokinetic data, and clinical trial evidence across major pain conditions in order to summarize the current evidence for, or against, efficacy and safety for pain. A synthesis of published information was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, and other databases, integrating findings from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and pharmacology reviews on CBD (independent of combination products where possible) and pain of any etiology. Preclinical and mechanistic data support plausible physical analgesic pathways for CBD, including receptor modulation, indirect enhancement of endocannabinoid tone via fatty-acid-binding-protein (FABP) inhibition, and anti-inflammatory effects. However, translation to clinical benefit has been inconsistent. In the largest meta-analysis of cannabinoids for pain, cannabinoids reduced chronic pain and improved sleep quality, but effect sizes fell below predefined minimally important clinical differences, and cannabinoids showed no benefit for acute or cancer pain, while increasing non-serious adverse events. CBD randomized trials in knee osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia, and acute low back pain have consistently failed to separate from placebo, whereas smaller/lower-quality trials and observational surveys report subjective benefit. Safety data increasingly point to dose-dependent hepatotoxicity risk. Despite strong biological plausibility and considerable consumer use, current high-quality evidence does not support CBD monotherapy as an effective analgesic across most pain conditions studied to date. Safety monitoring, particularly of liver enzymes at higher doses, is warranted.

papers.title: Hybrid sleep-wake states in psychosis: Examining a comprehensive array of unusual sleep and dream experiences in patients with psychosis compared to non-clinical controls.
papers.abstract: Psychosis has been likened to dream-like mentation permeating waking, with hallucinatory experiences, flawed logic, and salience of one's internal world over sensory perception. Some exceptional dream and sleep experiences have been viewed as representing hybrid states between sleep and waking, for example, dreams of falling/flying, dreams of awakening, lucid dreams, sleepwalking, hypnagogic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis. Several of these phenomena have been associated with psychopathological distress in general, and schizotypy and dissociative experiences in particular - dimensional manifestations of core experiences in psychotic disorders. To better understand sleep-wake mechanisms in psychosis, we wished to examine a host of sleep and dream experiences in patients with psychotic disorders. N = 75 patients were compared to n = 72 non-clinical controls on various exceptional sleep/dream experiences, as well as several universal dream themes. The clinical group had poorer sleep quality, and elevated dream phenomena including a general sleep experiences factor (e.g., awakening dreams, falling/flying dreams), lucid dreams, and hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, even when accounting for sleep quality. Dreams of persecution and grandiosity were elevated in the clinical group, but grandiosity seemed to be confounded by atypical antipsychotic medication use. We exploratorily examined differences between affective and non-affective psychosis but those analyses are limited by sample size. To conclude, researching dreams may shed light on blurred boundaries between wake and sleep in psychosis.

papers.title: De-escalating Therapy in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea After Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist-Induced Weight Loss: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Incretin-based therapies now achieve weight reduction of a magnitude previously attainable only through bariatric surgery and have demonstrated substantial reductions in the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) in adults with obesity-related obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Sleep services are consequently managing growing numbers of patients who undergo rapid, substantial weight loss while established on positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy, and who ask whether that therapy can be stopped. No guideline addresses this question. This narrative review synthesises three literatures that have developed largely in isolation: the relationship between weight change and OSA severity, the efficacy data for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin agonists in OSA, and the experimental PAP withdrawal literature. Across randomised trials and meta-analyses, there is consistent agreement that incretin therapy reduces AHI, body weight and blood pressure, with effect magnitude varying by agent, dose and baseline adiposity. There is, however, material disagreement on three questions directly relevant to de-escalation: whether the effect is wholly weight-mediated, whether AHI reduction translates into reduction in cardiovascular risk, and what proportion of patients achieve genuine disease remission as opposed to severity reduction. Approximately half of participants in the largest trial did not reach a severity threshold at which PAP would ordinarily be considered unnecessary, and withdrawal studies demonstrate recurrence of obstructive events and adverse haemodynamic change within days of stopping therapy. This review proposes a structured, reversible and documented framework for reassessment rather than ad hoc discontinuation and identifies the evidence gaps that must be closed before de-escalation can be considered evidence-based practice.

papers.title: Corollary discharge dysfunction in auditory verbal hallucinations: N100 suppression measured with semi-dry electrodes.
papers.abstract: Corollary discharge dysfunction in patients with auditory verbal hallucinations (AVH) is reflected in failure to attenuate the N100 event-related potential. Previous research has shown mixed findings regarding N100 suppression and hallucination severity, generally using broad symptom scales rather than AVH-specific measures. This study investigated corollary discharge and its relationship with comprehensively characterized auditory hallucinations. Corollary discharge was investigated in 14 patients with persistent auditory hallucinations and 15 healthy controls using an EEG paradigm using semi-dry electrodes where participants self-generated sounds in a "talk" condition and listened to playback in a "listen" condition. N100 suppression was calculated as the peak-amplitude difference (μV) between talk and listen in the 60-150 ms window. Auditory hallucinations were assessed with the Psychotic Symptom Rating Scales Auditory Hallucination Subscale (PSYRATS-AHS). Between-group analysis of the fronto-central ROI (Fz-Cz) showed a statistically non-significant trend toward greater N100 suppression in healthy controls compared to AVH patients (p = 0.095, Cohen's d = 0.64). N100 suppression showed significant negative correlation with hallucination severity in the AVH group (r = -0.54, p = 0.047). Hallucination severity is related to impaired corollary discharge mechanisms, supporting its role as a mechanistic basis for auditory hallucinations. The preliminary correlation with PSYRATS-AHS suggests potential value in using symptom-specific assessment tools in research on auditory hallucinations, warranting replication in larger samples.

papers.title: Normative data of laser evoked potentials using Nd:YAP laser.
papers.abstract: To establish a robust multi-centre normative database for Nd:YAP laser-evoked potentials (LEPs) across distal and proximal stimulation sites, and to quantify the impact of laser spot size (energy density) and demographic factors on LEP parameters. One hundred nine healthy adults (57 females) were recruited from three centres (Geneva, Lyon, Saint-Etienne). Nd:YAP laser pulses were delivered with a 3-mm beam (Centre 1) or 4-mm beam (Centres 2-3). LEPs were recorded from standard EEG sites (including Fz/Cz/Pz and contralateral temporal leads). Stimulation sites included hand dorsum (n = 109), foot dorsum (n = 80), thigh and upper neck (both n = 43). N1, N2, and P2 latencies and amplitudes were measured and normal limits estimated as mean ± 99.9% confidence interval. ANCOVA (age-corrected) tested spot-size effects; repeated-measures ANOVA tested site effects; correlations assessed age/height associations. The vertex N2-P2 complex was consistently recorded across centres and sites (100% for hand, thigh, neck; ∼97% for foot). N1 detection was less consistent, particularly with larger spot size and at the foot. Smaller spot size (higher energy density) yielded shorter N2/P2 latencies and larger N2-P2 amplitudes for hand stimulation, and shorter P2 latency for foot stimulation. Sex and height showed no significant effects. Increasing age was associated with longer N2/P2 latencies and reduced N2-P2 amplitudes for distal sites, with minimal age effects at proximal sites. This study provides the most comprehensive Nd:YAP LEP normative dataset to date, including distal and proximal sites and spot-size-specific reference limits. These data support standardized, high-specificity clinical interpretation of LEPs for assessing small-fibre and spinothalamic pathway dysfunction.

papers.title: Selective mGlu1 Receptor Activation Restores Cortical Inhibitory Tone and Improves Cognitive Performance in a Subchronic Phencyclidine NMDA Hypofunction Model.
papers.abstract: Deficits in prefrontal cortex (PFC) inhibitory transmission are thought to underlie the cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia that remain untreated by current pharmacotherapies. The metabotropic glutamate 1 (mGlu1) receptor, a subtype of the mGlu receptor family, is a promising therapeutic target because its activation enhances inhibitory transmission in the PFC through the excitation of somatostatin-expressing GABAergic (gamma-aminobutyric acidergic) interneurons (SST-INs). We used a subchronic phencyclidine (PCP) NMDA receptor antagonist mouse model, mGlu1 positive allosteric modulators (PAMs), and mice with selective deletion of mGlu1 receptors from SST-INs to examine the cell type-specific role of mGlu1 signaling in cortical inhibition and cognition. We used ex vivo whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology to assess inhibitory transmission in the PFC, and cognitive performance was evaluated using tests of working memory and novel object recognition. Subchronic PCP treatment impaired inhibitory synaptic transmission in the PFC, particularly onto layer V pyramidal neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens. Pharmacological activation of mGlu1 restored inhibitory drive and reversed PCP-induced deficits in working memory and novel object recognition. Importantly, selective deletion of mGlu1 receptors from SST-INs abolished the ability of mGlu1 activation to restore cortical inhibition and cognitive function, demonstrating that these receptors are required for the therapeutic effects of mGlu1 PAMs. These findings identify SST-IN-expressed mGlu1 receptors as critical regulators of prefrontal cortical inhibition and cognition. Positive allosteric modulation of mGlu1 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for treating cognitive deficits associated with schizophrenia by restoring inhibitory circuit function.

papers.title: Prevalence of night eating syndrome and associated factors among students at Kolej MARA Kuala Nerang: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Night eating syndrome (NES) is an eating disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of night eating, morning anorexia and insomnia. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and association of NES with depression, anxiety, stress, sleep quality and eating disorders among students in Kolej MARA Kuala Nerang (KMKN). A cross-sectional study was conducted on 426 students in KMKN. The calculated minimum sample size was 119. A universal sampling method was used, and data on sociodemographic characteristics, NES, depression, anxiety, stress, sleep quality and eating disorders were collected through online self-reported validated questionnaires including the Night Eating Questionnaire; Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale-21; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; and Eating Attitudes Test- 26. Data were analysed using IBM SPSS version 22. The chi-square test was used to evaluate the association of NES with sociodemographic characteristics and other factors (P<0.05). A total of 275 students responded (men: 55.6%, women: 44.4%), with 50.9% studying at the Foundation of Science and 49.1% at the Foundation of Science and Technology (FIST). The majority had mild-to-severe depression (56.4%) and anxiety (65.5%); 26.2% were stressed, and 10.2% engaged in NES. NES was not significantly associated with sex, age, monthly pocket money or body mass index. A significant number of students with NES were from the FIST (P=0.036). The factors significantly related to NES were depression (P=0.003), anxiety (P=0.021), stress (P<0.001), poor sleep quality (P=0.001) and risk of eating disorders (P=0.003). NES should be screened among at-risk college students to ensure they receive appropriate treatment.

papers.title: Acute Psychosis and Dissociative Syndrome Following Binge Recreational Nitrous Oxide Use: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Recreational nitrous oxide (N2O) inhalation is increasingly prevalent among young adults, but acute psychiatric presentations following short-term binge exposure remain poorly characterized. We report a case of a female in her early 20s with no prior history of psychotic illness who developed an acute psychotic and dissociative syndrome over three days at an outdoor music festival. Her presentation followed heavy recreational N2O and 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) exposure combined with sleep deprivation. On admission, she exhibited profound disorientation, inability to recognize close family members, polymorphic delusions, passivity phenomena, and auditory and olfactory hallucinations, requiring involuntary psychiatric hospitalization. Diagnostic workup revealed normal brain and cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a normal electroencephalogram (EEG) without epileptiform activity or slowing. Serum homocysteine was moderately elevated (25.2 µmol/L) alongside a low-normal vitamin B12 concentration (270 pg/mL), consistent with N2O-induced functional cobalamin deficiency; both markers normalized following parenteral vitamin B12 and oral folic acid supplementation. During inpatient stay, treatment with risperidone was followed by progressive neutropenia, which fully resolved after cross-titration to aripiprazole. She gradually regained full insight, was discharged on day 12, and remained free of psychotic symptoms at her three-week outpatient review. This case suggests that short-term binge N2O exposure, together with MDMA and sleep deprivation, may contribute to severe neuropsychiatric presentations without chronic use; it illustrates the value of measuring homocysteine rather than relying solely on serum B12 levels; and highlights potential hematological adverse effects during antipsychotic initiation.

papers.title: Laser-Based Rejuvenation of the Upper Airway: A Novel Non-Surgical Approach to Habitual Snoring.
papers.abstract: Introduction: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of Erbium-Doped Yttrium Aluminium Garnet (Er: YAG, 2940 nm), combined with a long-pulse Nd: YAG laser, in mitigating habitual snoring. Methods: Thirty patients participated in the single-arm prospective study, receiving approximately 20,000 pulses of the Er: YAG laser directed at the target sites using a patterned beam from the PSO3X handpiece in Long Pulse (LP) mode, followed by long-pulse Nd: YAG irradiation of the submental and lateral neck region. Treatments were administered on days 0, 15, and 45. The treatment response was evaluated through subjective methods, including the Snore Outcomes Survey (SOS) and the Spouse/Bed Partner Survey (SBPS). Anatomical enhancement was assessed using the Mallampati classification before each session and nine months subsequent to the final session. Results: The mean Mallampati class decreased from 3.50±0.68 to 2.43±0.73. Statistically significant alterations were observed in the SOS and SBPS scores, which increased from 47.10±11.34 to 66.22±11.18 and from 44.38±16.22 to 63.11±14.64, respectively. Older age showed a borderline correlation with the Mallampati class, whereas weight and BMI did not; patients with lower baseline SOS scores tended to improve more. Conclusion: In this single-arm pilot study, the combined Er: YAG and Nd: YAG protocol was well tolerated and was associated with improvements in habitual snoring; controlled trials are required to confirm its efficacy in the early management of snoring.
papers.journal: Journal of lasers in medical sciences

papers.title: Astrocyte molecular rhythm disruption in nucleus accumbens promotes increased binge-like drinking in mice.
papers.abstract: Alcohol misuse is a leading cause of preventable death worldwide. Chronic alcohol is associated with disrupted circadian rhythms, yet molecular mechanisms linking circadian rhythm dysregulation and alcohol consumption are poorly understood. Current FDA-approved treatments for alcohol use disorder (AUD) do not target molecular rhythms or sleep-wake cycles. Mammalian circadian rhythms are regulated by transcription-translation feedback loops that regulate expression of 'clock genes' (e.g., Arntl encoding for BMAL1). Both human and rodent studies demonstrate associations between clock gene variants and changes in reward-seeking behavior. Evidence suggests astrocytes, non-neuronal brain cells with cell-autonomous rhythms, may regulate both circadian rhythms and reward. In the nucleus accumbens (NAc), a region responsible for modulating alcohol- and reward-related behavior, over 43% of the astrocyte transcriptome is expressed rhythmically. However, no studies to date have investigated roles of NAc astrocyte rhythmicity in regulating alcohol drinking. We used AAV8-Gfap-Cre to functionally ablate molecular rhythms in NAc astrocytes of BMAL1 floxed mice. Two-bottle choice (2BC), drinking-in-the-light (DIL), and drinking-in-the-dark (DID) assessed alcohol drinking. Behavioral assays included locomotor response to novelty, sucrose preference, and social interaction. Disrupting molecular clock function in NAc astrocytes increased binge-like drinking during both DIL and DID paradigms ( d = 1.44), but not with any other drinking paradigm or behavior. This study carves out a unique role for astrocytes in controlling the temporal organization of reward circuitry and susceptibility to binge-drinking. Future studies will investigate clock-controlled astrocyte mechanisms, such as glutamate uptake and ATP release, that may underlie binge-like drinking behavior.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology

papers.title: The effectiveness of sound-based interventions on promoting sleep quality in hospitalized patients: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Sleep quality strongly affects hospitalized patients' recovery, yet pain, anxiety, and environmental factors such as noise and light frequently disrupt it. Sound-based therapies offer a promising, non-pharmacological approach, but their effectiveness has not been comprehensively synthesized. This systematic review examined fifteen studies (2012-2026, 2024 patients, mostly intensive care settings) evaluating sound-based interventions, including calming music, nature sounds, and white noise, on sleep quality. Intervention duration and timing varied widely, from brief five-minute sessions to continuous overnight administration, and sleep quality was most often measured using validated questionnaires. Despite substantial heterogeneity, sound-based interventions were associated with an overall improvement in sleep quality, although effect sizes varied considerably and several studies showed no significant benefit. These findings support the potential of low-cost, non-pharmacological sound interventions to improve sleep in hospital settings, while underscoring the need for further research to clarify which intervention characteristics drive effectiveness.

papers.title: Convergent and Distinct Transcriptional Signatures in Suicide, Bipolar Disorder, and Major Depressive Disorder.
papers.abstract: Globally, a person dies by suicide every 40 seconds, underscoring a major global public health concern. In the United States, suicide is the second leading cause of death among individuals aged 10-34 years. Suicide is a complex, multifactorial phenomenon influenced by genetic and epigenetic factors and is strongly associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD). However, the extent to which their molecular signatures converge or diverge across disorders and brain regions remains incompletely understood. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of suicide, MDD, and BD transcriptomic studies in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible studies used human postmortem brain tissue, reported a complete genome-wide transcriptomic list of differentially expressed genes (DEG), and compared suicide decedents with psychiatric non-suicide individuals diagnosed with the same underlying disorder. Regarding BD, studies comparing affected individuals to unaffected controls were included. Single-cell and peripheral-blood studies were excluded because unavailable for suicide. Curated suicide and BD DEG datasets were integrated with a published bulk transcriptomic dataset of MDD. We identified both shared and disease-specific molecular signatures across suicide, BD, and MDD, and identified DEGs shared across brain regions and those that were region-specific. A total of 276 genes were shared across all three conditions, implicating cellular stress, hypoxia (VEGFA, ADM, NDRG1, DDIT4), immune and inflammatory signaling through TNFα/NF-κB (IL1B, ICAM1, NFE2L2) and IL6-JAK-STAT3 pathways (STAT3, SOCS3, IL1R1m OSMR), complement activation (CIR, SERPiNA1, LGALS3), extracellular matrix remodeling (COL4A1, SERPINH1, PLOD2), and unfolded protein response (BAG3, WFS1, MTHFD2). Suicide-associated DEGs were prominently downregulated, and involved metal-ion homeostasis, stress responses, synaptic regulation, and circadian pathways, whereas BD showed downregulation in synaptic and vesicle-related processes alongside region-specific metabolic dysregulation. MDD exhibited changes in RNA processing, ribosomal function, and protein synthesis. Genetic integration revealed that 133 genes shared between BD and MDD had gene variants associated with the corresponding condition per GWAS. Transcription factor analysis identified 20 regulatory factors with altered activity across all three conditions despite differences in their predicted downstream targets. Overall, these findings suggest that suicide, MDD, and BD share aspects of their molecular and regulatory pathophysiology while exhibiting distinct patterns, including in a region-specific manner.
